Or has it? Cary Coglianese argues that Schechter Poultry (if not Panama 
Refining) is actually consistent with all the many subsequent cases that have 
upheld broad delegations, at least in their results (if not in all their re^omng). 
Most nondelegation opinions focus on whether the statute imposes sufficiently 
specific criteria for how the agency should exercise whatever power is 
delegated to it (hence the focus on whether the statue provides an intelhpble 
principle”). If the specificity of such criteria is the only dimension by whmh a 
delegation should be measured, then it does seem Schechter Poultry has been 
silently overturned, as several subsequent cases have upheld delegations with 
criteria like “public interest” that are no more intelligible than those in NIRA 
section 3. But Coglianese contends that delegations should be (and at key 
points have been) measured along additional dimensions. The main additior^ 
dimension is the extent of the agency’s power if it is exercised, that is, t e 
potential range of regulated parties and of regulated activities. Against this 
background, Coglianese argues that the delegated power in Schechter 
Poultry—when measured not only by the looseness of its criteria but also by 
other dimensions such as the greatness of its extent was different from and

In Schechter Poultry, * * * the problem was not merely that the 
National Industrial Recovery Act contained few, if any, meaningful 
standards for the exercise of authority; the problem also lay with the 
broad extent of the lawmaking powers given to the President. The 
Court stressed that the President’s authority under the Act 
encompassed a “wide field of legislative possibilities” and relate[d] 
to a host of different trades and industries, thus extending the 
President’s discretion to all the varieties of laws which he may deem 
to be beneficial in dealing with the vast array of commercial and 
industrial activities throughout the country.” * * *
